rationale: Within-site AUROC means differences between cohorts in protein levels (pre-analytics, instrument runs) are pure noise for the pooled classifier. I'm adding one step: after imputation, centre each protein on its per-site median. The median is computed label-free over all train+test samples of that site. This should let the L2 logistic regression learn the within-cohort AD contrast and not fit site offsets.

With about 110 training samples and about 1,000 proteins, a fully learned L2 model is noisy, so I'm adding one fixed-sign prior-biology score and averaging it with the logistic-regression score. The score combines CSF markers from Bader 2020 and other literature that rise with tau/neurodegeneration (SMOC1, YWHAG, the glycolytic enzymes PKM/ALDOA/MDH1/ENO1/GAPDH, CHI3L1, SPP1, NEFL, GFAP) and synaptic markers that fall (NPTX2, VGF, NPTX1). Because no weights are fitted for this score, it should not overfit, and it should add a stable within-site signal.

Two ideas in this change are new and still need checking: that the larger panel adds signal, and that summarising by module beats a flat average. The averaged literature panel is the most stable part of the model, but with only about 10 proteins passing the 70% filter it is noisy. I'm adding the other members of the same CSF AD modules: more 14-3-3 proteins, more glycolysis enzymes, the neuronal-injury markers MAPT/NRGN/GAP43, and more synaptic secretory proteins that fall in AD. Each module is averaged first and the module scores are then averaged. That way a big module, like glycolysis, doesn't outweigh small but specific markers like SMOC1, NEFL and NPTX2.

Low-abundance CSF markers such as NEFL, SMOC1, GFAP and NPTX2 are often missing in more than 30% of DIA runs, so the 70% filter shared with the logistic regression silently removes them from the fixed panel. This change selects the same panel proteins at a looser ≥30% threshold, used for the panel only. Missing values still get half-minimum imputation, so non-detection counts as "low abundance", which fits the abundance-dependent missingness. The goal is to recover the most AD-specific signals without adding any fitted weights.

I'm adding a diagonal linear discriminant (nearest-shrunken-centroid) score as a second data-driven component. With about 110 samples and about 1,000 correlated proteins, independence-rule classifiers (Bickel & Levina; Tibshirani's PAM) are often more stable than a full-covariance logistic regression. This score averages the train-standardized proteins, each weighted by its soft-thresholded effect size, so only about 40 proteins contribute. The data-driven half of the blend becomes the mean of logistic regression and this score, and the fixed panel keeps its 0.5 weight.

The current per-sample median is taken over whichever proteins happen to be quantified in that sample. Because missingness depends on abundance, a sample that misses more low-abundance proteins gets an inflated median, so every protein in it is shifted down. That bias then feeds both the logistic regression and the fixed panel. This change computes each sample's median only over a fixed reference set of proteins quantified in nearly all samples (chosen without labels, over all items), which removes the bias.

Blood from a traumatic lumbar puncture is the main pre-analytical confounder in CSF proteomics. Red blood cells are rich in the glycolytic enzymes (GAPDH, ENO1, PKM, ALDOA, MDH1) that the fixed panel counts as "AD-up", and leaked plasma raises many other proteins. I'm building an erythrocyte-contamination score from hemoglobins, CA1/CA2, PRDX2, CAT and similar proteins, removing those proteins from the features, and regressing the score out of every remaining protein. The regression slopes are fitted on the training fold only. Both the logistic regression and the panel then see contamination-free levels.

Last round, removing the erythrocyte-contamination axis helped. The other big non-AD source of variation in CSF proteomics is leakage across the blood–CSF barrier: albumin, immunoglobulins, A2M, haptoglobin, fibrinogen and similar proteins that are made almost only in the liver or by B-cells. That leakage rises with age and with many non-AD neurological conditions. I'm reusing the same score-and-regress step for a fixed panel of these plasma proteins (slopes fitted on train only, the proteins themselves dropped), so the logistic regression and the fixed panel see brain-derived levels without this confound.

Barrier leakage and immunoglobulin load are now removed as one combined "plasma" axis. I'm splitting it into two axes, removed one after the other: liver-derived proteins (albumin-quotient-like leakage) and immunoglobulins (which also carry intrathecal B-cell IgG/IgA/IgM synthesis in inflammatory non-AD controls). These two vary independently in CSF, so a single averaged score only partly removes each one.

With about 110 samples, a few extreme protein values can steer both the L2 logistic regression and the 14-protein unweighted panel average. These extremes come from contamination spikes, single-run quantification glitches and very low half-minimum imputed values. This change clips each standardized, confounder-corrected protein to ±3 SD before both models. It is a label-free robustness step: the bulk of the within-site AD contrast stays intact, and no single sample–protein value can dominate a score.

L2 strength is still fixed at C=0.05, which was chosen before the blood-contamination and barrier-leakage removal and the ±3 SD clipping changed the feature structure. This change picks C on the training fold only, using grouped inner CV (with `groups_train`) and the same within-site AUROC as the harness. The full label-free preprocessing is refit inside each inner fold so nothing leaks, and the fixed-sign panel half of the blend stays the same.

The L2 logistic regression penalizes all ~1,000 proteins equally, even though prior biology says the 14 literature CSF AD markers are much more likely to carry signal. This change multiplies those panel proteins by 2 (after correction and clipping) before the logistic regression only, so their effective penalty drops 4-fold. That amounts to a wider Gaussian prior on those weights: the model can still learn their sign and size from the data, while the other proteins stay strongly shrunk. The fixed-sign panel score is computed from the unscaled values, exactly as before.

Scoring is within site, but the pooled L2 logistic regression is trained across four cohorts whose AD prevalence differs. Some of its weights therefore go to proteins that only separate sites. This change adds weakly penalized one-hot site indicators during training (similar to stratified/conditional logistic regression) and drops them at prediction, so protein weights only reflect the within-cohort AD contrast. Unlike round 1's per-site median centring, this does not shift features by a site median that depends on how many AD cases each site has.

rationale: This reruns the round-13 idea with the crash fixed. The crash happened because the site column came back as a pandas Arrow array, which can't be indexed as `s[:, None]`; site labels are now converted to a plain numpy string array first. During logistic-regression training only, I add weakly penalized one-hot site indicators (scaled ×5, so their L2 penalty is about 25× weaker) and drop them at prediction. Because scoring is within site, the protein weights should then capture the within-cohort AD contrast rather than differences in AD prevalence between cohorts.

Remove a third, analytical confounder axis: identification depth, i.e. the log number of proteins quantified per sample. Depth reflects injection amount, run quality and instrument sensitivity. Because missingness depends on abundance, low-depth runs get many low half-minimum imputed values and shifted intensities near the detection limit, and that is not AD biology. As with the blood and plasma axes, I regress the standardized depth score out of every protein, with slopes fitted on the training fold only.

Hemoglobins and other erythrocyte markers are often not quantified at all in clean CSF, and that missingness itself means "no blood". The shared ≥70% filter therefore probably drops the most specific contamination markers, so the blood axis is currently built from weaker proxies like CA1/PRDX2/CAT. This change builds the blood-contamination and plasma-leakage scores from marker proteins quantified in ≥30% of training samples, with half-minimum imputation so non-detection counts as low. Both scores are then regressed out of every protein jointly, with slopes fitted on train only, and all marker proteins are dropped from the features.

The fixed panel is currently a plain signed mean of 11 "up" markers and 3 "down" markers, so the synaptic markers (NPTX2/VGF/NPTX1) get only 3/14 of the weight. That matters because in clinical non-AD controls with other neurological diseases, the general neuronal-injury and glycolytic "up" markers are less specific, while synaptic decline is more AD-specific. This change turns the panel into a balanced log-ratio, mean(up) − mean(down), so the two groups weigh equally. If either group has no proteins passing the filter, it falls back to the signed mean.

Rounds 7 and 8 removed blood-contamination and barrier-leakage axes, and both helped. This change adds the third quality-marker panel from Geyer et al. 2019: platelets (PF4, PPBP, TLN1, ITGA2B/ITGB3, GP1BA, F13A1, THBS1, MYL9, TPM4 and others). Platelet proteins enter CSF through traumatic taps and in vitro clotting, separately from red-cell lysis. They are then scored and regressed out of the remaining proteins with the same train-only slope step, so both the logistic regression and the panel see platelet-free levels. I haven't run this, so I have no new Dev score for it yet.

Rounds 7, 8 and 18 each gained by removing a known pre-analytical axis (red blood cells, plasma leakage, platelets). This change removes one more: skin and handling contamination (epidermal keratins KRT1/2/9/10, desmosome proteins, dermcidin and similar). It varies with how each lab and run handled samples, not with AD. It goes through the same step as before: build a score, regress it out of every remaining protein with slopes fitted on the training fold only, then drop the marker proteins. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score yet. If fewer than two keratin proteins pass the 70% filter, the step does nothing.

Rounds 11 and 12 suggest that picking C with nested CV on about 110 samples is too noisy, so I'm averaging over several prior strengths instead of picking one. The single L2 logistic regression at C=0.05 is replaced by the mean of standardized decision functions at C ∈ {0.01, 0.05, 0.25}. This should make the data-driven half of the blend less sensitive to the one fixed C without fitting anything new to labels. I haven't run this change, so there is no Dev score for it yet.
